title: Encapsulation
summary: Hide an object's state behind methods so its rules cannot be broken from outside.

steps.title: The problem with public state
body: Here is an account anyone can ruin:
Every line of code in the program is now responsible for keeping the balance sensible. One mistake anywhere and the data is wrong, with no clue who did it.
**Access modifiers** decide who may touch a member:
- `private`: only code **inside the same class** can use it.
Members are `private` when you write no modifier at all. Private fields are usually named with a leading underscore.

steps.explain: `_balance` is private, so only code inside `Account` can touch it. The outside world has to go through `Deposit` and `GetBalance`.

steps.title: Private setters and invariants
body: A property can have a public `get` and a **private** `set`. Everyone can read it. Only the class can change it.
public decimal Balance { get; private set; }
throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
Now `Withdraw` is the only door, and the door has a guard.

A rule that must always hold, like *the balance is never negative*, is called an **invariant**. Encapsulation means the class protects its own invariants, so the rest of the program cannot break them even by accident.
> **Tip:** `ArgumentException` says *the value you passed is wrong*. `InvalidOperationException` says *the value is fine, but the object is in no state to do this*.

steps.prompt: Outside code may read `Quantity` and call `Remove`, but must not set `Quantity` directly.
steps.explain: The setter is private, the method is public, and the method checks the rule before changing anything.

steps.prompt: This version returns `false` instead of throwing. What does it print?
code: public decimal Balance { get; private set; }
steps.explain: The first withdrawal is refused and changes nothing. The second succeeds. The balance can only move through `Withdraw`, so it can never go below zero.

steps.title: Close the holes
prompt: This `Account` works, but anyone can put it into any state. Close the holes **without changing the names**.
1. `Owner` can only be set by the constructor.
2. `Balance` can be read by anyone but set only inside the class.
3. `Deposit` throws `ArgumentException` when `amount` is zero or negative.
4. `Withdraw` throws `ArgumentException` when `amount` is zero or negative, and `InvalidOperationException` when `amount` is more than the balance.
solution: public decimal Balance { get; private set; }
throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
template: var dojoA = new Account("Maya");
Dojo.Eq("Owner comes from the constructor", "Maya", dojoA.Owner);
Dojo.Check("Owner cannot be set from outside", typeof(Account).GetProperty("Owner") is { } dojoOwner && dojoOwner.SetMethod?.IsPublic != true, "Owner should be a property with no public setter");
Dojo.Check("Balance cannot be set from outside", typeof(Account).GetProperty("Balance") is { } dojoBal && dojoBal.SetMethod?.IsPublic != true, "Balance should be a property with a private setter");
dojoA.Deposit(100m);
Dojo.Eq("Deposit(100) raises Balance to 100", 100m, dojoA.Balance);
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("Deposit(0) throws ArgumentException", () => dojoA.Deposit(0m));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("Deposit(-5) throws ArgumentException", () => dojoA.Deposit(-5m));
Dojo.Try("Withdraw(30) lowers Balance to 70", () => { dojoA.Withdraw(30m); Dojo.Eq("Withdraw(30) lowers Balance to 70", 70m, dojoA.Balance); });
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("Withdraw(-1) throws ArgumentException", () => dojoA.Withdraw(-1m));
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("Withdraw(500) throws InvalidOperationException", () => dojoA.Withdraw(500m));
Dojo.Eq("Balance is still 70 after the refused calls", 70m, dojoA.Balance);
Dojo.Try("Withdraw(70) can empty the account", () => { dojoA.Withdraw(70m); Dojo.Eq("Withdraw(70) can empty the account", 0m, dojoA.Balance); });
{{CODE}}
hints: Two of the fixes are in the property declarations: `{ get; }` and `{ get; private set; }`.
A guard is an `if` followed by `throw new ArgumentException("...");` at the top of the method.
In `Withdraw`, check `amount <= 0` first, then `amount > Balance` with `InvalidOperationException`. Only then subtract.

steps.title: The four access levels
body: `public` and `private` do most of the work. Two more exist:
| `internal` | any code in the same project |
| `protected` | this class and classes that inherit from it |
- A **class** written with no modifier is `internal`. That is fine for an app, and it matters when you write a library for other projects.
- A **member** written with no modifier is `private`.
- `protected` only makes sense with inheritance, which is two lessons away.
The habit to build: start with `private`, and open something up only when other code really needs it. It is easy to make a member public later. Taking it back breaks everyone who used it.

steps.title: readonly, and hiding collections
body: A `readonly` field can be assigned only where it is declared or in the constructor. After that it is locked.
throw new ArgumentException("Item name is required");
- `readonly` locks the **reference**. `_items` will always point at the same list, but the list itself can still grow.
- The list is `private`. If it were public, any code could call `cart.Items.Clear()` or add an empty name, walking straight past the check in `Add`.
So the cart exposes what callers need (`Count`, `Add`) and keeps the list to itself.

steps.prompt: Inside the `Cart` class, `_items` is declared `private readonly List<string> _items`. Which statement is true?
options: `_items.Add("Mug")` works, but `_items = new List<string>()` in a method does not compile
Both work, because `readonly` only affects code outside the class
steps.explain: `readonly` stops the field being pointed at a different list. It says nothing about what happens inside the list.

steps.title: An inventory that cannot go wrong
prompt: Write a class `Inventory` that tracks units in stock per SKU (a product code such as `"TEA-01"`). Keep the data in a **private** field; a `Dictionary<string, int>` works well.
- `void AddStock(string sku, int quantity)`: throws `ArgumentException` when `quantity` is zero or negative
- `void RemoveStock(string sku, int quantity)`: throws `ArgumentException` when `quantity` is zero or negative, and `InvalidOperationException` when there is not enough of that SKU
- `int GetStock(string sku)`: units of that SKU, or `0` for a SKU it has never seen
- `int TotalUnits`: a property anyone can read and nobody outside can set, holding the total units across all SKUs
The invariant: no SKU ever has negative stock, and `TotalUnits` always matches.
starter: public void AddStock(string sku, int quantity)
public void RemoveStock(string sku, int quantity)
solution: private readonly Dictionary<string, int> _stock = new Dictionary<string, int>();
public int TotalUnits { get; private set; }
public void AddStock(string sku, int quantity)
throw new ArgumentException("Quantity must be positive");
public void RemoveStock(string sku, int quantity)
throw new ArgumentException("Quantity must be positive");
template: var dojoInv = new Inventory();
Dojo.Eq("GetStock of an unknown SKU is 0", 0, dojoInv.GetStock("TEA-01"));
Dojo.Eq("TotalUnits starts at 0", 0, dojoInv.TotalUnits);
Dojo.Try("AddStock(\"TEA-01\", 10) stores 10", () => { dojoInv.AddStock("TEA-01", 10); Dojo.Eq("AddStock(\"TEA-01\", 10) stores 10", 10, dojoInv.GetStock("TEA-01")); });
Dojo.Try("adding 5 more makes 15", () => { dojoInv.AddStock("TEA-01", 5); Dojo.Eq("adding 5 more makes 15", 15, dojoInv.GetStock("TEA-01")); });
Dojo.Try("a second SKU is tracked separately", () => { dojoInv.AddStock("MUG-07", 4); Dojo.Eq("a second SKU is tracked separately", 4, dojoInv.GetStock("MUG-07")); });
Dojo.Eq("TotalUnits is 19 across both SKUs", 19, dojoInv.TotalUnits);
Dojo.Try("RemoveStock(\"TEA-01\", 6) leaves 9", () => { dojoInv.RemoveStock("TEA-01", 6); Dojo.Eq("RemoveStock(\"TEA-01\", 6) leaves 9", 9, dojoInv.GetStock("TEA-01")); });
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("AddStock with quantity 0 throws ArgumentException", () => dojoInv.AddStock("TEA-01", 0));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("RemoveStock with quantity -2 throws ArgumentException", () => dojoInv.RemoveStock("TEA-01", -2));
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("removing 5 mugs when there are 4 throws InvalidOperationException", () => dojoInv.RemoveStock("MUG-07", 5));
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("removing an unknown SKU throws InvalidOperationException", () => dojoInv.RemoveStock("NOPE", 1));
Dojo.Eq("refused calls change nothing: mugs still 4", 4, dojoInv.GetStock("MUG-07"));
Dojo.Eq("TotalUnits is 13 at the end", 13, dojoInv.TotalUnits);
Dojo.Check("Inventory has no public fields", typeof(Inventory).GetFields().Length == 0, "Keep the dictionary private");

Dojo.Check("TotalUnits cannot be set from outside", typeof(Inventory).GetProperty("TotalUnits") is { } dojoTotal && dojoTotal.SetMethod?.IsPublic != true, "TotalUnits should be a property with no public setter");
{{CODE}}
hints: Start with `private readonly Dictionary<string, int> _stock = new Dictionary<string, int>();` and `public int TotalUnits { get; private set; }`.
Write `GetStock` first using `ContainsKey`. Then `AddStock` can say `_stock[sku] = GetStock(sku) + quantity;` and it works for new and known SKUs alike.
In `RemoveStock`, do both checks before changing anything: `quantity <= 0`, then `quantity > GetStock(sku)`. Remember to adjust `TotalUnits` in both methods.
